description: Fig. 1 is a single-panel, dual-axis plot summarising the yield stress and ductility of polycrystalline, as-cast or annealed Fe–Al alloys as a function of Al content. The x-axis is "Aluminium content (%)" from 0 to 40 (gridlines every 10). The left y-axis is "Yield Stress (MPa)" from 0 to 800 (gridlines every 100); the right y-axis is "Ductility (%)" from 0 to 40 (gridlines every 5). Two labelled series are overlaid: "Yield Stress" (solid line, filled triangles, read on the left axis) and "Ductility" (dashed line, filled circles, read on the right axis). The yield-stress curve climbs almost linearly from near zero at 0% Al to a sharp maximum just above the 700 MPa gridline near 26% Al, then plunges to about the 300–350 MPa level at 28–30% Al and stays roughly flat with a slight rise up to 40% Al. Ductility is broadly inverse: about 35% at 13–14% Al, falling to near 25% at 20% Al, down to a minimum close to the 2% gridline at 26% Al, with a small local maximum of roughly 5–6% at 28% Al, then a slow decline toward ~1–2% at 40% Al. The figure demonstrates the inverse yield-stress/ductility relationship and an anomalous, small ductility peak near 28% Al. Title strip reads "Yield stress, Ductility - Al content".

observations.observation: The figure is a dual-axis plot with 'Aluminium content (%)' (0–40) on the x-axis, 'Yield Stress (MPa)' (0–800) on the left y-axis and 'Ductility (%)' (0–40) on the right y-axis, with the title strip 'Yield stress, Ductility - Al content'.
The 'Yield Stress' series (solid line, filled triangle markers) rises from near 0 MPa at 0% Al to a sharp maximum just above the 700 MPa gridline near 26% Al.
The yield-stress curve falls steeply between about 26% and 28% Al to roughly the 300–350 MPa level, then remains approximately flat with a slight rise up to 40% Al.
The 'Ductility' series (dashed line, filled circle markers) falls from about the 35% gridline at 13–14% Al to a minimum close to the 2% gridline at about 26% Al.
A small local ductility maximum of approximately 5–6% (between the 5 and 10% gridlines on the right axis) is visible at about 28% Al, after which ductility declines slowly to ~1–2% at 40% Al.
The caption states the data are taken from Refs. [2,5,8] and the present study.

The caption/source states the figure shows yield stress and ductility of polycrystalline, as-cast or annealed Fe–Al alloys versus Al content from essentially pure Fe to the intermetallic FeAl with 40% Al (atomic percent).
The citing text reports a steadily increasing yield stress with Al content up to 25% Al, a rapid fall at 25–28% Al, and little change or a slight increase over the 30–40% Al range.
The citing text describes ductility as showing an essentially inverse relationship to yield stress: a rapid fall to 25% Al, a slight maximum at 28% Al, and a steady slow fall thereafter.

The citing text states all data come from essentially thermally-relaxed as-cast materials with coarse grain sizes and no solute or precipitates, so grain-size, solution and particle effects do not importantly modify strength.
The citing text attributes the small ductility peak near 28% Al to the peak in work hardening rate over the 26–30% Al composition range, where flow stress is relatively constant.
The citing text notes that over about 25–30% Al, where DO3 order was possible, materials were generally considered in the slowly cooled state with good B2 order and moderate DO3 order.

sample_hints: polycrystalline, as-cast or annealed Fe–Al alloys
